doc.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999

title: What the first Los Angeles band taught her
summary: Studio players who doubled shaped her writing; she grew as a person and learned the logistics and finances.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: I think the Los Angeles band were creatures of the first band. It was very important in many different ways but one thing was that because of the saxophone player, all of them doubled because most of them were studio players. So because they doubled, I utilized that. And that became a trademark of my writing. So everything is sort of like it goes both ways. If they didn’t double I wouldn’t have it written. And a long time ago when I was in Japan I heard somebody’s music, a woodwind, maybe third stream or something, it was sort of fast, and I heard — but to me that wasn’t jazz, and if I were writing for woodwinds I would not write like that. So that was the opportunity for me to write. So it was the first band that was a very important band. Also the first band was very important for me because I never touted so many musicians in my life. It was after I came to this country, a trio or quartet, and no more than that. So it was a totally different story with so many musicians you have to deal with it. And pianists tend to be — at least I am — tend to be paranoia. And it took me a long time to get over taking everything personally. And so I grew up as a human being with the first band I think. So that was a very important band.
Not only musically then but in a lot of ways.
It must have been a struggle just economically and logistically for that many people — to get them to rehearsals.

Well everyone came to rehearsals because they liked it. No one got paid — still don’t today. You know we do rehearsals but no one gets paid. In New York you pay your own subway token or what have you. And in Los Angeles it’s the same. Everybody came to rehearse. And on Wednesday morning that was something for them to do, and later on when people said I would like to have a band to have a concert here, and I was so inexperienced so I will book a hotel that was more than the payroll. So the musician would lose money, and things like that. It was really a disaster. For a long time, I had to
do everything — airplane arrangements, hotel arrangements, bus arrangements. So it was a learning process for me, and I think with the first band paid a lot of dues.
